eras.title: Marks that stand in for memory
eras.intro: The earliest writing in this exhibit is not literature. It is bookkeeping: a way to hold a quantity outside anyone's head.

artifact.name: Administrative account tablet
artifact.line: Clay, Sumerian, Jemdet Nasr period, ca. 3100–2900 BCE
facts: The Met dates the tablet to ca. 3100–2900 BCE and gives its medium as clay, 4.5 × 6.85 × 1.6 cm.
met-tablet
The Met says it likely records grain handed out by a large temple.
met-tablet
The earliest tablets, from around 3300 BCE, used pictographs and numerals to record economic information.
met-tablet
The symbols stood for nouns, mostly commodity names, and a few basic adjectives, but carried no grammatical elements.
met-tablet
Because these texts served as memory aids, the Met says they are hard to read today.
met-tablet

kept: Commodity names and numerals: what was handed out.
lost: Grammar. The Met says the system had no grammatical elements, which is part of why the tablets are hard to read now.
eras.reading: In this room memory is a ledger. It is kept outside the person, and it records what was owed or given, not what anyone felt.

eras.title: A library gathered for a king
eras.when: 7th century BC (reign dates differ by source)
eras.intro: A ruler orders the world's written knowledge brought to one place. What survives is not the library as it stood, but what its ruin left behind.

artifact.name: Fragment K.3999, Library of Ashurbanipal
artifact.line: Neo-Assyrian clay tablet fragment, 7th century BC, from Kouyunjik
facts: The British Museum describes K.3999 as a fragment of a Neo-Assyrian clay tablet carrying an omen about the padanum (the 'path'), a groove on the left lobe of the liver.
It measures about 12.38 × 8.57 × 3.17 cm and was excavated at Kouyunjik by Sir Austen Henry Layard and others.
The British Museum project page says the library held 'Over 30,000 clay tablets', with Assyrian and Babylonian scholarly texts.
bm-library
The blog says Ashurbanipal sent agents across the empire to gather texts and wanted a copy of every worthwhile book.
bm-who
The project page says excavators did not find a library frozen in time: it had been sifted and deliberately smashed, and the pieces dumped around the palaces at Nineveh.
bm-library
The library was damaged when Nineveh fell in 612 BC, according to the project page.
bm-library

kept: Scholarly texts, some copied faithfully and some edited into new forms, and 'library labels' (colophons) that researchers are now classifying.
lost: The library as an intact collection. The project page says its research aims to establish how many tablets there were, where they came from and how much survives, so those figures are still being worked out.
decides: A king and his agents decided what to collect; the blog says Ashurbanipal wanted a copy of every worthwhile book.
eras.reading: Here memory is a collection, and a collection is a decision about what counts as worth having. It is also fragile: the same power that gathers it can leave it broken.

eras.title: The question asked three times
eras.intro: A government asks its subjects fixed questions and writes down the answers. The record becomes the thing people argue from.

artifact.name: Domesday Book (Great and Little Domesday)
artifact.line: Survey and valuation of landed property in England, end of the 11th century
facts: The National Archives says William the Conqueror ordered the survey at Christmas 1085 and it was carried out in 1086.
tna-domesday
Commissioners held sworn inquests in local courts, asking fixed questions of local men.
tna-domesday
For each property each question was asked three times: for the time of Edward the Confessor (5 January 1066), when granted by King William, and in 1086.
tna-domesday
The guide says Domesday is 'not a census': the people named are almost all landholders.
tna-domesday
Most returns went into Great Domesday. Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex are in a separate, smaller volume, Little Domesday.
tna-domesday
The original can 'no longer be consulted except in very rare circumstances'; the guide points readers to facsimiles, translations and websites.
tna-domesday

kept: Who held land, how it was used, and how that had changed since the Conquest in 1066.
lost: Most people. The guide says the survey is not a census and the people named are almost all landholders.
decides: The king ordered the survey; commissioners put the fixed questions to local men.
eras.reading: Memory becomes an instrument of administration. It records what the state needs to know, in the shape the state's questions allow.

eras.title: Memory by multiplication
eras.intro: Instead of guarding one precious copy, you make many. Survival becomes a matter of numbers.

artifact.name: The Gutenberg Bible (Biblia latina)
artifact.line: Printed with moveable metal type; Library of Congress holds a complete vellum copy
facts: The Library of Congress says Johann Gutenberg printed it in Mainz, first available about 1455.
loc-gutenberg
It calls it 'the first book printed with moveable metal type in Western Europe', and notes that moveable metal type was used in Korea nearly a century earlier.
loc-gutenberg
About 180 copies were printed: 145 on paper and 35 on vellum.
loc-gutenberg
Forty-nine copies survived into the twentieth century, and 21 of those are complete.
loc-gutenberg
The Library of Congress copy is one of three complete vellum copies and sits in the Otto Vollbehr Collection.
loc-gutenberg

kept: About 49 of roughly 180 copies survived into the twentieth century.
lost: Roughly 130 copies by that count, which is this exhibit's subtraction of the Library's two figures; the Library does not state it.
eras.reading: Memory shifts from protecting a single object to spreading many copies. Even so, the Library of Congress figures show that most of the original print run did not survive.

eras.title: Deciding what to keep
eras.intro: Modern archives do not keep everything. Selection is a stated, governed act, and it is the quiet centre of institutional memory.

artifact.name: Selection for permanent preservation
facts: Under the Public Records Act 1958, bodies responsible for public records must arrange for selection of those worth keeping permanently.
tna-selection
Selection decides which records pass to The National Archives or another appropriate place of deposit, and applies to records in all formats.
tna-selection
The guidance says selection looks for records of historical value to an organisation or society.
tna-selection
Generic selection criteria and Operational Selection Policies help apply the collection themes to individual departments or agencies.
tna-selection

kept: Records judged to have historical value, in any format.
lost: Records not selected. The guidance describes the selection process; it does not here say how much is not kept.
decides: Public record bodies identify records, under the supervision of The National Archives.
eras.reading: Here the question 'what is worth remembering?' has an office, a policy and a legal basis. Forgetting is also a managed outcome.

eras.title: The web remembers, partly
eras.intro: Everything seems permanent online, yet digital things depend on machines that change. Preservation has to be done on purpose.

artifact.name: The Wayback Machine
artifact.line: Archived versions of web sites, run by the Internet Archive
facts: The Internet Archive's help page says it began archiving the web in 1996; about five years later, with over 100 terabytes and a dozen crawls done, the service became public.
ia-wayback
It captures publicly available web pages. Standard HTML archives well; dynamic pages that depend on forms, JavaScript or the originating host do not keep their original functionality.
ia-wayback
Not all sites are collected. Password-protected pages, form-only pages and pages on secure servers are not archived, and pages may be excluded by robots exclusions or at a site owner's request.
ia-wayback
The Library of Congress said in 2010 that digital possessions depend on technology, and that as technology changes and becomes obsolete they need active management to stay available.

kept: Publicly available pages that the crawlers reached.
lost: Password-protected pages, secure-server pages, personal email and chat (unless public), and anything excluded by robots rules or owner request.
decides: Crawlers collect, but site owners can exclude pages through robots exclusions or direct request.
eras.reading: Memory becomes a service that has to be maintained. Whether something survives depends on who can reach it, and on who chooses to keep it reachable.

eras.title: Memory as pattern
eras.intro: A system trained on vast amounts of text can answer questions without being a library. This room asks what 'remembering' should mean for it. It does not answer.

artifact.name: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
artifact.line: Brown et al., arXiv:2005.14165, submitted 28 May 2020
facts: The paper has 31 authors; the first is Tom B. Brown. It was submitted to arXiv on 28 May 2020.
brown-2020
It introduces GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters.
brown-2020
The authors evaluate it without any weight updates, specifying tasks and examples only through text.
brown-2020
The abstract says the work raises methodological concerns tied to large web-scraped training data.
brown-2020

eras.open: Does a model that was trained on web text 'remember' that text, in any sense that a tablet, a library or an archive does? This exhibit makes no claim; the abstract read here does not address it.
eras.reading: The earlier rooms kept particular objects. This one is about a system whose relation to its sources is less clear, which is why it is posed as a question. For a longer essay on this theme, see 'We Are All Archives Now' in the Published Research library.

notes: Dates for Ashurbanipal's reign differ between two British Museum pages: 668–631 BC on the project page and 669 to c. 631 BC on the blog. Both are shown rather than reconciled.

The British Museum blog says Ashurbanipal 'amassed hundreds of thousands of tablets' and that about 30,000 are now in the Museum; the project page says the library held 'Over 30,000 clay tablets'. These are different framings, not a settled count.
The blog says the first fragments were found in 1849; the project page says the library was excavated between 1851 and 1932. This exhibit does not reconcile them.
The 'In this room' interpretations are the exhibit's own reading. They are marked as such and are not claims from the sources.
